planting.note: Mount on cork bark or a slab, or grow in a shallow clay pot with very coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix; this Central American species stores water in its broad, flattened pseudobulbs and needs bright light and a brief dry period between waterings rather than constant moisture.

directions: Mount this species on bark or cork, or grow it in a shallow pot with chunky, open mix, since its rounded, flattened pseudobulbs give it the common name 'turtle shell orchid' and store enough moisture to tolerate brief dry spells between waterings. Native to lowland forests from Mexico through Panama and into northern South America, it produces tall, branching spikes in spring carrying dozens of small, bright yellow flowers marked with reddish-brown at the base of the lip. Provide bright, filtered light rather than deep shade, since insufficient light is the most common reason this species fails to flower well in cultivation. Allow the mount or mix to dry noticeably between waterings and reduce watering further in winter to mimic its natural dry season.
sources: American Orchid Society

planting.note: Pot in a small, fast-draining epiphytic bark mix or mount on cork; this Brazilian species produces long, arching to pendent flower spikes and benefits from a basket or hanging position so the inflorescence can develop unobstructed.

directions: Grow in a slatted basket or pot of coarse bark so the long, arching flower spikes can hang freely, since this Brazilian species' stems often cascade well beyond the pot rim once mature. Each spring the spikes carry numerous waxy, heavily textured yellow flowers densely blotched in reddish brown, with a lightly fragrant scent on warm days. Water generously and feed regularly while new growths and roots are actively developing, then ease off once pseudobulbs mature to encourage flower initiation. Bright, filtered light and good air movement keep the thin-textured leaves free of spotting and help this free-flowering species build the multiple pseudobulbs needed for a full display.
sources: American Orchid Society

common_name: Jones' Oncidium (Fragrant Pansy-Faced Orchid, trade name Oncidium jonesianum)

planting.note: Mount on cork or a slab with little or no additional medium, since this South American species has thick, semi-terete leaves adapted to bright light and quick drying and dislikes a constantly damp root zone.

directions: Still widely sold in the trade under its older name, Oncidium jonesianum, this compact species from Brazil, Paraguay, Bolivia, and Argentina is best mounted on cork or bark rather than potted, since its thick, fleshy, semi-cylindrical leaves rot easily if kept wet. Short, arching spikes in summer and fall carry two to five large, strongly fragrant white flowers overlaid with maroon-brown bars near the center, giving the flower its pansy-faced look. Water or mist frequently during active growth but allow the mount to dry within hours each time, and provide very bright light to keep the thick foliage compact and well colored. Reduce watering further in winter to encourage the next flowering cycle.
sources: American Orchid Society

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or warm greenhouse specimen in bright, indirect light in a coarse, fast-draining bark mix; this Philippine limestone-cliff species needs warm, humid, stable conditions year-round and resents being disturbed once established.

directions: Pot in a chunky, fast-draining bark mix and provide bright, filtered light rather than direct sun, since this multiflora-type slipper orchid from the Philippines grows naturally on shaded limestone cliffs with excellent drainage. Each inflorescence carries two to five flowers with a striped maroon-and-cream dorsal sepal and dramatically long, twisted, ribbon-like lateral petals that continue to lengthen for several weeks after opening. Keep warm and humid year-round, since this lowland species has little tolerance for cool temperatures, and water regularly without letting the mix become waterlogged. Established clumps produce an increasingly showy display as multiple growths reach blooming size together.
sources: American Orchid Society - Paphiopedilum Culture Sheet

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fine-bark terrestrial orchid mix with added limestone chips or grit; this Yunnan limestone-cliff species forms spreading clumps via short stolons and prefers a brief cooler, drier rest in winter.

directions: Discovered on limestone cliffs in Yunnan, China, in the late 1970s, this species quickly became famous for producing a single, clear golden-yellow flower per stem, a color almost unheard of in the genus at the time. It spreads slowly by short stolons into multi-growth clumps, each with compact, mottled foliage, so use a wide shallow pot rather than a deep one. Add limestone chips or crushed coral to the bark-based mix to buffer the pH toward the alkaline conditions this species prefers in the wild. Provide bright, indirect light and a slightly cooler, drier rest after flowering to encourage strong new growths the following season.
sources: American Orchid Society - Paphiopedilum Culture Sheet

common_name: Concolor Slipper Orchid (Pale Yellow Spotted Paphiopedilum)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a fine-bark terrestrial orchid mix with added limestone chips; this limestone-cliff species from Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, and Vietnam prefers warm, buoyant conditions and a slightly drier rest in winter.

directions: A compact, clump-forming slipper orchid from limestone outcrops of mainland Southeast Asia, this species bears pale creamy-yellow flowers finely speckled with purple-maroon dots across both the dorsal sepal and the rounded pouch. Its softly mottled leaves form low rosettes, making it well suited to shallow pans where offsets can spread into an eventual multi-growth specimen. Add limestone chips or crushed coral to the bark mix to approximate the alkaline substrate of its native cliffs, and keep humidity high while avoiding standing water around the crown. Flowering typically occurs in summer, with blooms lasting several weeks under stable warm conditions.
sources: American Orchid Society - Paphiopedilum Culture Sheet

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or pot of coarse, fast-draining bark in bright, indirect light; this Myanmar, Thailand, and Yunnan species grows naturally in mossy tree crotches and sends its long flower spike downward, so an elevated or hanging position shows the blooms best.

directions: Grow this multiflora slipper orchid in a hanging basket rather than a standard pot, since its arching inflorescence of four to six flowers droops downward and is best displayed at eye level or above. The long, dark, twisted petals and glossy, hairy-margined pouch give each flower an almost spidery appearance quite different from the rounder, single-flowered paphiopedilum species. Provide bright, filtered light, consistent warmth, and high humidity, mimicking the mossy tree crotches of evergreen forest where it grows naturally epiphytically or on rocks. Water regularly but let the mix approach dryness between soakings, and avoid moving or repotting plants more than necessary since root disturbance can delay flowering for a full season.

planting.note: Pot in a coarse, bark-based cymbidium mix in bright light with some direct morning sun; this Himalayan species needs a pronounced cool-night, warm-day temperature swing in fall to initiate its winter-to-spring flower spikes.

directions: Native to mid-elevation forests of the Himalaya and southwestern China, this large-growing species produces arching spikes of up to a dozen broad, strongly fragrant flowers in pale yellow-green marked with a red-streaked lip. Grow in a coarse bark mix in a large pot with excellent drainage, giving as much bright light as possible without scorching the long, strap-like leaves. A fall temperature drop of fifteen to twenty degrees between day and night is essential to trigger flowering, so plants kept too warm or too shaded commonly produce lush foliage but few or no spikes. This species has long been a key parent behind the large, fragrant yellow and green standard cymbidium hybrids grown worldwide.
sources: American Orchid Society

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring and pot into a fast-draining terrestrial orchid mix of fine bark, perlite, and leaf mold, growing in bright shade; this widespread Chinese species has long been cultivated as a traditional pot plant valued for fragrance over flashy color.

directions: One of the classic 'fragrant grass-leaf' cymbidiums long cultivated across China, this terrestrial species forms dense tufts of narrow, finely serrated, grass-like leaves that stay attractive year-round. In spring, upright spikes carry several yellow-green flowers finely marked with maroon spotting on the lip, valued more for their sweet, penetrating fragrance than for size or color. Grow in bright shade in a fast-draining terrestrial mix, keeping the roots evenly moist but never soggy, and divide crowded clumps every few years once growth slows. Unlike the large hybrid cymbidiums bred for show-quality flowers, this species and its many traditional cultivars are prized in East Asian horticulture primarily for scent and foliage form.
sources: American Orchid Society

common_name: Giant Golden Cymbidium (Iridioides Himalayan Boat Orchid, syn. Cymbidium giganteum)

planting.note: Pot in a large container of coarse, bark-based cymbidium mix in bright light; this large Himalayan and southwestern Chinese species needs a strong fall temperature drop and plenty of root room to flower reliably.

directions: This large, vigorous species from the Himalaya and southwestern China produces broad, arching strap leaves to three feet long and, in fall, upright to arching spikes of large, powerfully fragrant yellow-green flowers heavily striped with red on the lip. Grow in a generously sized pot of coarse bark mix, since root-bound plants flower more reliably than recently repotted ones, and provide bright light with some gentle direct sun to keep foliage compact. A pronounced cool-night, warm-day swing in autumn is needed to initiate spikes, mirroring the seasonal shift in its native mid-elevation forests. This species has contributed its large size and fragrance to numerous standard cymbidium hybrids bred over the past century.
sources: American Orchid Society

planting.note: Mount on a slab or hang bare-root in a slatted basket with minimal medium so the thick aerial roots have maximum air exposure; this Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam species needs very bright light and daily root wetting followed by rapid drying.

directions: A monopodial, essentially leafless-root epiphyte like other Vandas, this species needs very bright light and roots that are wetted thoroughly and then allowed to dry within a few hours, grown bare-root in a basket or mounted on a slab rather than potted in soil. Waxy, ivory-yellow flowers with faint tessellation open in spring and release a strong, sweet fragrance most noticeable in the evening, a trait that distinguishes it from the day-fragrant blue Vanda coerulea. Provide warmth and high humidity year-round along with strong air movement around the roots to prevent rot between waterings. This species has been used in breeding for fragrance and for its distinctive ivory-and-yellow coloring in warm-growing Vanda hybrids.
sources: American Orchid Society

planting.note: Mount on a slab or grow bare-root in a slatted basket with minimal medium; this compact Vanda from the Philippines, Taiwan, and the Ryukyu Islands tolerates somewhat cooler conditions than most tropical lowland Vandas but still needs very bright light.

directions: Smaller-growing and somewhat more temperature-tolerant than many Vanda species, this plant produces fragrant, waxy flowers striped in yellow-brown over a paler ground with a contrasting white lip, borne on upright spikes that can appear more than once a year. Grow bare-root in a basket or mounted on a slab with maximum air exposure around the roots, watering or misting frequently in warm weather and allowing roots to dry within hours each time. Provide very bright light, approaching full sun in mild climates, to keep growth compact and encourage repeat flowering. Its naturally compact habit and relative cold tolerance for the genus have made it a useful parent in breeding smaller, more weather-tolerant Vanda hybrids.

common_name: Fringed Star Orchid (Comb Orchid, Ciliare Epidendrum)

planting.note: Mount on bark or cork, or pot in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix in bright, filtered light; this wide-ranging species from Mexico to South America and the Caribbean tolerates a range of conditions but flowers best with strong light and good air movement.

directions: Long-lasting, greenish-white to cream flowers open from clustered spathes at the tip of each cane, their narrow petals and sepals surrounding a distinctive three-lobed lip deeply fringed into comb-like segments, which gives this widespread species its common names. Flowers release a sweet fragrance most noticeable after dark, attracting night-flying moth pollinators, and a single inflorescence can continue producing new blooms over many months. Mount on bark or grow in a small pot of coarse, open mix, providing bright filtered light and good air circulation to prevent the thin canes from rotting. Water regularly during active growth and reduce slightly in cooler months, since this adaptable species tolerates a wider range of conditions than many epiphytic orchids.
sources: American Orchid Society

common_name: Night-Scented Star Orchid (Dama de Noche Epidendrum)

planting.note: Mount on rough bark or pot in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix; this species native to southern Florida, the Caribbean, Mexico, and Central and South America can grow outdoors year-round in the warmest zones but is usually grown as a protected patio or greenhouse plant elsewhere.

directions: Each starry, long-lasting flower has narrow, twisted, pale green to cream petals surrounding a prominent three-lobed white lip, opening from a terminal cluster at the tip of slender reed-like canes. True to its name, the flowers release a strong, sweet fragrance after dusk to attract night-flying moths, and a single plant can bloom intermittently for much of the warm season. Mount on rough bark or grow in a small pot of coarse, open mix, giving bright filtered light and consistent moisture during active growth. In its native south Florida range it can be grown outdoors on trees year-round, while in cooler areas it does best as a container plant brought under cover for winter.
sources: American Orchid Society

common_name: Lemon-Scented Orchid (Yellow Nodding Encyclia, syn. Cattleya citrina)

planting.note: Mount on cork or a slab and hang so the pendent growths can droop naturally; this Mexican oak-forest species from mid-elevation, seasonally dry habitats needs very bright light and a pronounced dry rest after flowering.

directions: Native to oak and pine-oak forests at moderate elevation in central Mexico, this species grows naturally hanging from branches, and its pendent habit means it should always be mounted rather than potted upright. Waxy, lemon-yellow flowers nod downward in pairs or singly from the apex of new growths and carry a strong, pleasant citrus fragrance, a trait reflected in both its scientific and common names. Provide very bright light approaching full sun along with excellent air movement, and allow the mount to dry thoroughly between waterings, since this species comes from a habitat with a pronounced dry season. Reduce watering further after flowering to mimic that seasonal rest and encourage strong new growths the following year.
sources: American Orchid Society

common_name: Warty-Sepaled Lady of the Night (Tuberculata Brassavola)

planting.note: Mount on cork bark or a tree fern slab, or grow in a slatted basket with coarse bark; this Brazilian, Paraguayan, and northeastern Argentine species tolerates bright light similar to Brassavola nodosa but has narrower, more pendent foliage.

directions: Closely related to the better-known Brassavola nodosa, this species has narrow, semi-terete, slightly pendent leaves and star-shaped summer flowers in greenish-yellow, with sepals and petals roughened by small raised warts or tubercles that give the species its name. A fringed white lip contrasts with the textured yellow-green segments, and like its relatives the flowers release a strong, sweet fragrance after dark to attract night-flying moths. Mount on cork or bark and grow in bright light with good air movement, watering generously during active growth and allowing the mount to dry between soakings. This species has been used alongside Brassavola nodosa in hybridizing for nocturnal fragrance in Cattleya-alliance crosses.

common_name: Garbancillo (Michoacan Laelia, Mexican State Flower Orchid)

planting.note: Mount on bark or cork, or grow in a clay pot with very coarse, free-draining medium; this high-elevation oak-forest species from central Mexico needs excellent drainage and a pronounced dry-warm rest after flowering, similar to Laelia anceps culture.

directions: This slow-growing species from oak forests of central Mexico, particularly Michoacan, where it is honored as a regional floral emblem, bears some of the largest and showiest flowers in the genus, typically solitary or paired, three to five inches across in rich rose-purple with a deeper magenta, trumpet-shaped lip. Wild populations have declined from habitat loss and collection, so only purchase plants propagated by reputable nurseries rather than wild-collected material. Mount on bark or grow in a clay pot with very coarse medium, since the thick roots need outstanding drainage and air movement, and provide bright light with a dry, cooler rest after flowering to mimic its native seasonal cycle. Growth is slow, with new pseudobulbs and roots forming over a long season before the plant reaches flowering size.
sources: American Orchid Society

common_name: Day of the Dead Orchid (Flor de Todos Santos, Autumn Laelia)

planting.note: Mount on bark or cork, or grow in a clay pot with very coarse, free-draining medium; this Mexican highland oak-and-pine forest species needs excellent drainage, bright light, and a dry-warm summer rest similar to Laelia anceps.

directions: Named for its reliable autumn bloom around the Day of the Dead and All Saints holidays in its native Mexico, this high-elevation species sends up spikes of three to seven fragrant flowers in shades of lavender-rose to purple, each with a darker, trumpet-shaped lip marked in deep magenta and yellow. It grows naturally on oaks and pines in seasonally dry highland forests, so it needs outstanding drainage, bright light, and good air movement in cultivation, whether mounted on bark or potted in very coarse medium. Water generously while new growths develop in the warmer months, then taper off sharply once pseudobulbs mature to trigger the fall flowering cycle. Like Laelia anceps, this species tolerates brief cool spells once dry, making it a good candidate for sheltered outdoor culture in the mildest zones.
sources: American Orchid Society
